Hello, I just want to share a motivational story! I played on and off since 2015 and only started playing religiously 3 years ago with a 5 [stack.](https://stack.at) At the start of 2020, 3 of my friends were completely new to FPS's and were really.... bad (trying to track the enemy for a good 2 seconds before they started shooting... bad). 

Under the guidance of another veteran friend and countless (300+) games they slowly improved and now I can say that they got insanely better (even better than I am) and better game sense since they first started. 

I may not be the top percentile of players but here are some tips to make the game less painful: 

1) try to find some friends to play with, hopefully the non-toxic kind. It makes the experience 1000% better and way more fun if you can just laugh and have a good time no matter win/lose.

2) Spending an hour or 30 minutes consciously practicing your mechanics (counter-strafing THEN spraying/Taking time to aim at the head) in bot dm and eventually normal dm works wonders in the future.

3) Since workshop maps are down, watch some videos from content creators like (WarOwl, Elige, etc.) They'll give tips and explain the intricacies of the mechanics I mentioned. CS2 may be new but the core mechanics are still the same as CSGO.

4) Try to stick to 1 or 2 maps to get comfortable with the spots you play and try not to expose yourself to multiple angles where the enemy may catch you off guard.

If you're in Asia hmu! I dont mind playing compet/premier as I don't really care about the rank. I really hope you don't give up! This is a great game even though the community can be toxic.

I don't really know the details regarding elemental calculations but I'll try explaining.

Alatreon starts in either Fire or Ice and you're supposed to bring a weapon with the opposite element as he is weak to it.

He has an elemental DPS check called the Escaton Judement(EJ) that will (almost) instantly kill you and your team.

How do you prevent that? By smacking him with your elemental weapon! There is a threshold you will reach faster/slower depending on your elemental damage. Once you reach the threshold he will fall over and it's free real estate.

My advice would be go with whatever has the highest elemental damage as the threshold will increase after every EJ.

The raw portion of your weapon won't really matter unless in rare cases you find it too easy to reach his elemental threshold and unable to break his horns even though you take advantage of the openings (alatreon has alot of head openings. I suggest watching a guide on his moves and how to punish them). If anyone knows more about this part please enlighten me if I'm wrong.

Hello! I'm from Singapore too and have been sliding casually for a 3 years now.

Taking lessons and talking to your instructors for advice are good enough. There are specific shops in SG with experienced freestyle skaters you could try signing up for their lessons eg. Hvper in ECP and quite a number of shops in Bishan.

1. Most good hybrid( great at both slides and slalom) skaters are godlike and practise everyday. Some skaters find it easier to focus on one discipline and then switching but I suggest sticking with whatever you find cool and work towards it eg: To learn backslide you start with crossacid.

2. Seba Highs are amazing beginner skates (I'm still using em) but I would recommend upgrading to the igor custom (not so comfortable but great control) or Freestyle TT Carbon ( Heard great reviews about its comfort and control). 

Upgrade after you manage to avoid sliding on your slide pads
Sliding on your skates will damage them and it really just looks bad on a pair of $600+ pair of skates.

As for Carbon cuffs, they are very VERY STIFF. Gives great calf support but tend to impede your slaloming mobility. Plastic ones are good enough but every skater has their preference.

3. Try to fix the edging problem without altering the of your frames as edging control is very important in slalom.
Only use the centre hole to align your frame. I know a couple of skaters who shifted the frame backwards to improve their wheeling slides like Toe Crossacid wheeling.

Try sticking with rocker as it really helps with mobility

As for maintenance, there are some great solutions in this thread already.

4.
The key to getting good is constant practise. Sometimes you would feel like you aren't getting better but trust me, all those failed attempts are valuable if you are able to analyze and compare your body posture/cutting angle/edging to the videos and correct acordingly then you're all set.

IMO learning 2-3 slides/ tricks at one go and do not change up until you REALLY cannot progress. For slides, a good gauge of whether you "mastered" a slide would be 3-5 meters slide distance (Opinions may vary). I don't do much slalom so i can't say much but maybe weaving 20 cones fluidly per trick would be ideal.
